Hausse des fugues dans les centres jeune: Rise in runaways from youth centres: employees denounce a “broken system”
Après la montée du mot-clic #Survivanted: After the hashtag #SurvivantedeCentreJeunesse took off, employees are now speaking out against the abuses in youth centres.
Bonjour, c’est Lela avec Loubna et Chris: Hello, it’s Lela with Loubna and Chris!
La première partie de cette enquête dévo: The first part of this investigation presents the accounts of Shayna, a girl placed in the Laval youth centre, as well as those of her mother and several young women who passed through the same facility. All of them denounce degrading living conditions and mistreatment.
Dans cette seconde partie, nous vous pro: In this second part, we share the accounts of people who work within the youth protection system. It is a different perspective that supports the young women’s allegations while also offering some context. These professionals are not authorized to speak to the media and are therefore anonymous, to prevent possible repercussions on their careers.
Contrairement au premier article pour le: Unlike for the first article, for which neither the minister responsible for Social Services, Lionel Carmant, nor the management of the CISSS de Laval agreed to give us an interview, this time we were able to put our questions to the new national director of Youth Protection: Lesley Hill.
<strong>Fatiguées d’être montrées du doi: Tired of being blamed, worn down by a system they consider failing, and frustrated at not having the means to carry out their mission of protecting young people, a social worker, a youth centre teacher and a DPJ employee are speaking out. After Shayna’s testimony and the rise of the hashtag #SurvivantedeCentreJeunesse, they are now denouncing the abuses in these facilities, abuses that Director of Youth Protection Lesley Hill also acknowledges.
Depuis près d’un an, les fugues s’enchaî: For nearly a year, runaways have followed one after another at the Laval youth centre. According to the CISSS in question, 298 young people have run away over the past 10 months. That is the highest number since 2020. “We are seeing an even greater increase in runaways among girls in recent years,” says Lesley Hill, national director of Youth Protection.
Ni les rapports ni <l1>la Commission Lau: Neither the reports nor <l1>the Laurent Commission</l1> seem to have been enough to curb this phenomenon. While the reasons for these runaways are multifactorial, living conditions in youth centres push some to flee, as several young women who passed through the Laval youth centre told us <l2>in the first part of this investigation</l2>.
Elles ne sont pas seules à prendre la pa: They are not alone in speaking out. Despite the ban on communicating with the media, youth protection professionals are sharing their accounts. Like the young people, they are calling for awareness and rapid change.
Interrogée par La Converse, Leysley Hill: Questioned by La Converse, Lesley Hill, who was appointed last fall, does not deny the problems that exist within the institution. Convinced that this situation, which has dragged on for decades, is “unacceptable,” she promises to change things.
Centre jeunesse : « C’est vraiment le de: Youth centre: “It’s really the last resort”
La Converse s’est entretenue avec une em: La Converse spoke with an employee of the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ), whom we will call Florence* to protect her anonymity. Like many internet users, she discovered Shayna through the video the girl posted on TikTok on February 7. “It really hurt me, but I was really glad it was out there.”
Elle salue le courage de l’adolescente,: She praises the courage of the teenager, who spoke in front of the camera to denounce what she is going through at the Laval youth centre. “She has the right to speak up! I think young people need to talk about what they go through inside the system, and a social worker who is doing their job well shouldn’t worry about that,” she adds.
Le « système », Florence le connaît de l: Florence knows the “system” from the inside, since she is one of the people who must handle reports made to the DPJ and decide the fate of these young people. She always tries to avoid placing young people in youth centres. In her view, some children placed in these facilities don’t belong there.
Ces centres regroupent en effet des adol: These centres bring together teenagers who have committed offences; children who are victims of parental neglect, physical violence or sexual abuse; and children who no longer have parents to take care of them. “If you’re placed in a centre at 15 because you’re being abused by your father and your mother doesn’t believe you, you need someone to take care of you! Imagine the anger that creates, feeling alone at that moment, seeing workers who don’t help… You can’t feel like you’re there to be taken care of if your room looks like a prison cell!” Florence laments. According to the DPJ employee, the coercive culture of youth centres sends the wrong message to the young people placed there. “These kids really take in the idea that we want to punish them by putting them there and, honestly, I’m not going to argue that it doesn’t look like a pretty big punishment too!” Florence says, exasperated.
C’est ce qu’a vécu Laurie*, qui est aujo: That is what Laurie*, who is now 27, experienced. As a teenager, Laurie was placed in a youth centre for running away after her mother’s death. In her unit, she found near-carceral rules. She was not allowed to talk with the other young people without a social worker present. “I had just lost my mother and I got no support for that, no follow-up, no care.” She says she witnessed acts of mistreatment by centre employees. “You often hear screaming there… I remember a girl who didn’t want to be taken to the isolation room. Then there were really loud cries of pain, and when I saw her come back several hours later, she had bruises on her arms,” Laurie asserts. Despite her repeated requests to be placed in another facility, Laurie stayed in the youth centre for four long years. She left when she came of age. “I spent four years there, and nothing was done for me,” she says with regret.
Florence, elle, ne mâche pas ses mots en: Florence does not mince words about how little attention is paid in Quebec to the residents of youth centres: “Do we not care about young people? We really don’t care! People don’t care!” she exclaims.
« L’exploitation sexuelle, c’est invisib: “Sexual exploitation is invisible, whereas a guy shooting another guy in the street, we’ll see it and we’ll hear about it! A dead body is concrete, but sexual exploitation happens in silence…” she continues. “You have to understand that these are teenage girls in distress and a perfect guy shows up and offers them everything they want… Some go along with it. Sometimes we find them; sometimes it’s a vicious cycle: they run away again and so on… Others flee to the other end of Canada, where we never find them, and end up turning 18, living their lives in drugs or becoming sex workers.”
Sans modèle, sans schéma affectif sain d: Without role models, without any healthy model of affection around them, these young women lack the bearings they need to build themselves up. “Most of them would like to become architects or lawyers, but everything around them is already too broken for them to develop enough confidence and self-esteem,” the worker says. “The system contributes to that, with workers who change all the time and parents who aren’t able to take care of you. So you’re stuck there with kids who are always in crisis because you can’t calm yourself down, you fall into a kind of vicious cycle, you go crazy…”
Ces jeunes filles ont besoin d’un encadr: These young women need special support, but it is not always offered to them. “A novice social worker is just a free pass for them to run away, or to react more strongly because they feel misunderstood,” explains the DPJ professional. “It’s extremely frustrating to talk about your situation with someone who looks at you with fish eyes. These kids need very experienced workers.”
Florence l’affirme, le problème des cent: Florence says the problem with youth centres is systemic and begins with the hiring of staff. First, because the selection criteria are allegedly not high enough. “There should be skills tests and more thorough interviews to make sure we have employees who are capable of taking care of young people.”
Dans un contexte de pénurie de main-d’œu: In a context of skilled labour shortage, the psychosocial support Florence hopes for is rarely a reality. “It’s not an environment where social workers have time to do gentle interventions, even though the kids need them,” she explains. “It’s a system that is broken,” she says bluntly.
Elle nous raconte ses débuts difficiles: She tells us about her difficult beginnings at the DPJ, which required her to adapt quickly to the particular workings of this institution. “When I started working at the DPJ, I often struggled with the things I heard, the things my colleagues said. They weren’t aware of their biases and of what they were going to inflict on families because of their lack of education,” Florence confides. And she is categorical: the system has to change. “I’d like someone to come and shake it up, and for the government to have no choice but to act, to bring in skills tests and thorough interviews to make sure we have employees who are capable of taking care of young people.”
Lorsqu’on lui demande à quoi pourraient: Asked what better youth centres could look like, Florence closes her eyes and describes a welcoming gathering place: “It should be a big house, it shouldn’t look like a prison. It should be like a mansion, a place to live. Even if the [furniture] is fixed to the floor, there’s a way to make it nice, to personalize the place.”
Bas salaires, manque de moyens, violence: Low wages, lack of resources, violence – unattractive jobs in youth centres
Une employée d’un centre jeunesse, que n: A youth centre employee, whom we will call Hélène*, agreed to talk to us about her working conditions, despite fearing repercussions for her career. At 14, Hélène was also placed in a youth centre. She remembers being put in isolation and confined to her room for several days in a row. Some consequences were more severe. “I spent four months without being able to leave the building. It was a prison, and kids have no business being there,” she says. In her view, things have changed since the time she was under the state’s guardianship. “But it also brought a kind of structure into my life at a time when I needed it. I had bad company, I could have ended up in human trafficking if I hadn’t been placed in a centre.”
C’est pour mieux aider les jeunes qui se: It is to better help the young people who end up in centres that Hélène decided to return as an employee. But she believes that even the most dedicated teachers and social workers cannot do their jobs properly, given how heavy the workload is.
« Quand on est une travailleuse sociale: “When you’re a social worker and you’re responsible for 200 files instead of 60, you can never really be present for the kids,” the professional explains.
Dans un contexte où il faut sans cesse p: In a context where the most urgent needs must constantly be dealt with first, no gentle social intervention would be possible. “You stop seeing them as people, you focus on the need to manage them as quickly as possible so you can move on to the next one,” she admits bitterly. “These kids need love and attention. But in too many cases, they’re treated like numbers.”
La surcharge de travail, les salaires pe: Overwork, unattractive salaries, exposure to violence and the impossibility of carrying out their mission of protecting young people would push many youth centre workers to quit. Others try the experience before throwing in the towel, unable to bear the daily reality. That is the case of Marie*, who worked as a teacher in youth centres for years before leaving the field in 2015.
Selon elle, les coupes budgétaires et le: In her view, budget cuts and high staff turnover endanger both the young people and the adults responsible for their well-being. In 2013, while she was working in a youth centre in the Montréal region, the number of security guards in her unit was reduced. The next day, one of the youths punched her in the face.
Les accidents de travail aggravent les a: Workplace injuries worsen the absences of an already limited staff and create a climate of instability that is not conducive to children’s well-being, the former teacher points out. “In a five-day week, there would sometimes be a substitute teacher for three days,” Marie says. “The kids don’t know this person, they don’t trust them; we constantly impose this uncertainty on them at a time when they desperately need stability.”
Durant son passage dans les centres jeun: During her time in youth centres, she noticed a marked decline in the quality of the food and an obsession with budget cuts, which went as far as reducing the quality of the plastic used for the droppers used to administer medication to the young people.
Marie est toujours en contact avec d’anc: Marie is still in contact with former colleagues, who tell her the situation has only gotten worse. “Our social safety net is collapsing,” she laments. “Young people are being pushed to their limits. We take them out of their homes, we place them in a poorly organized, borderline chaotic environment, and it’s obvious to them that their well-being is not a priority.”
<strong>La nouvelle directrice nationale: The DPJ’s new national director admits systemic problems
Entrée en poste l’automne dernier, la di: Appointed last fall, the national director of the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse, Lesley Hill, is aware that she has inherited a network mired in difficulties. She has built a career in social services, has led several rehabilitation centres and sat on the Special Commission on the Rights of Children and Youth Protection, so she knows the institution and its cracks well.
Dès le départ, Lesley Hill reconnaît l’e: From the outset, Lesley Hill acknowledges “a lot of testimonies and a lot of issues” linked to youth centres, as well as an increase in the number of girls running away in recent years. The DPJ’s national director says she intends to bring about deep change. “It shouldn’t exist in Quebec, institutionalized young people… No young person should live their adolescence in a rehabilitation centre. Just the word ‘rehabilitation’ means: it’s temporary, you go there, you’re ‘rehabilitated,’ in quotation marks, and you leave,” she says.
La directrice rappelle que « les mesures: The director points out that “control measures should be exceptional, not routine,” and that they are “framed by law.” The use of these measures is indeed regulated. Section 118.1 of the Youth Protection Act states the following: “Force, isolation, any mechanical means or any chemical substance may be used as a measure of control of a person in a facility maintained by an institution only to prevent the person from inflicting injury on themselves or on another. The use of such a measure must be minimal and exceptional and must take into account the person’s physical and mental condition.”
Pourtant plusieurs témoignages décrivent: Yet several accounts describe isolation lasting many hours – 12 hours in the case of our witness Shayna – for reasons that have more to do with punishment than with safety. “I am absolutely against this type of practice. (...) One hour is the maximum desired, or tolerated, for a teenage girl. (...) It’s unacceptable to me. If there are young women who are still there, who are saying things like that, they need to file a complaint, or else I’ll ask my adviser who is already there, in Laval, to meet with them on site,” Lesley Hill commits. “It’s not compliant. After a runaway, when a young person comes back to the centre, she should be welcomed properly: see if she’s cold, give her some soup, something to eat, ask her why she ran away, what happened to her, and so on. So what’s clear is that an isolation room is not what’s needed!”
Selon la directrice de la DPJ, la straté: According to the DPJ director, the strategy of repression in youth centres must be replaced by a strategy of prevention and repair. “I think people are so busy trying to manage risk that they sometimes fall into methods that are truly too controlling. They’re caught up in this risk management. But personally, I’d rather we manage risk less, even if it means more runaways, and that we do more follow-up with the young people,” she explains. She believes this approach, while raising fears among some parents, would allow for better long-term support.
Depuis la <l1>vague de fugues de 2016</l: Since the <l1>wave of runaways in 2016</l1>, little seems to have changed, judging by the many accounts from young people and professionals.
À propos du Centre jeunesse de Laval, Le: Regarding the Laval youth centre, Lesley Hill says things will change. The question is when. “I think the leadership in Laval knows that things have to change. They’re taking action and they’re really moving. But you don’t bring about a change of culture by snapping your fingers. A change of culture is not quick,” says M<sup>s</sup>. Hill.
<em>« </em>Je suis en intervention au ce: “I’m doing an intervention at the Laval centre with the adviser (in December, Manon St-Maurice was appointed as external expert adviser; editor’s note) to review the whole way Laval uses what we call control measures: isolation, restraint (...) In Laval, this carceral living environment, if I had a magic wand, I would tear it all down and then rebuild something else… Management has a reconstruction plan and I think their vision is the right vision.” The project provides for the construction of small units, but it has been neither approved nor funded. It will therefore take many years before the Laval youth centre gets a second life.
De façon plus globale, la directrice veu: More broadly, the director wants to make significant changes. In youth centres, young people are placed in units: so-called “open” units, where they have the most freedom; “closed” units, with stricter supervision; and “secure” units, also called “high dynamic,” with total control over their every move. For 30 years, these units have been the subject of debate. The Laurent Commission has repeatedly questioned their legality.
« Je ne suis pas en train de dire que je: “I’m not saying I’m going to tear everything down or remove everything tomorrow, but children under 12, eventually, I don’t want to see them at all in rehabilitation centres,” says Lesley Hill. She hopes to create centres that are “much more open to the community”: “Yes, young people may run away and they may crash and burn, but we have to be there to pick them up, support them and accompany them. I really want our network to return to the core values of our professions, which are much more humanistic.”
À cet égard, M<sup>me</sup> Hill reconna: In this regard, M<sup>s</sup>. Hill acknowledges that staff recruitment is one of the areas that needs improvement. “Yes, the workers are young, and yes, things go off the rails. So every time things go off the rails, I expect an assessment of the situation within the institution to understand, and to try to improve,” she says without offering further detail.
Tout en rappelant que de nombreux jeunes: While noting that many young people speak of the help provided by certain dedicated educators or workers, she admits that more background checks and more screening of candidates are needed before any hiring. But is the institution really ready for a deep change in its methods?
Les problèmes de recrutement liés à la p: Recruitment problems linked to the labour shortage, the lack of appeal of social services jobs and gaps in background checks can sometimes lead to tragic situations. Several cases of sexual assault and abuse have marked recent years.
Le 19 octobre 2023, la Commission des dr: On October 19, 2023, the Quebec Human Rights and Youth Rights Commission opened an investigation following two reports of sexual abuse committed in 2021 by a student special education worker against teenagers housed at the Centre jeunesse de Laval. Last Tuesday, the Commission released its findings: “The Commission has reason to believe that the rights of the child (...) were violated by the Director of Youth Protection (DYP) at the CISSS de Laval.”
Après plusieurs mois d’enquête, la Commi: After several months of investigation, the Commission concluded that the DYP failed in its duty “to prioritize the child’s interests and ensure their protection.” It also faulted the DYP for an “incomplete and erroneous analysis of the situation of sexual abuse,” a lack of diligence, failure to follow certain processes, and a breach of its “obligation to communicate regularly with the child and thereby provide adequate social follow-up.”
Plusieurs recommandations sont formulées: The Commission makes several recommendations, starting with ongoing training for teams on how to intervene in situations of sexual abuse, a review of intervention practices, and the creation of assessment tools for teams.
Ce cas n’est pas isolé. En 2019, Benoit: This case is not isolated. In 2019, Benoit Cardinal, who murdered his partner Jaël Cantin the following year, allegedly used his position as a youth worker to sexually assault nine teenage girls, aged 13 to 17, at the Centre jeunesse de Laval. Six days before the murder, he had resigned from his position over “inappropriate behaviour.” These allegations were not presented at his trial for the murder of Jaël Cantin, the mother of his six children, for which he was sentenced to life in prison on appeal in 2021.
